title: Don’t sell an AI-written article before you choose its market
preview_markdown:
# Don’t sell an AI-written article before you choose its market

## The short answer

- AI can help turn writing work into something sellable, but an article without a market is inventory, not a product.
- Apify says its writing program pays $500 for an accepted article once it has been reviewed and prepared for publication. It asks for original, practical work tied to what the writer has built.
- TECHi’s free Author tier lists a one-million combined-follower threshold. Treat it as a conditional opportunity, not an entry-level pitch.

At 9:40 a.m., the draft is finally clean. The instinct is to publish it everywhere, then hope one of those places turns into income. That is where a lot of good material becomes an expensive pile of links.

Choose the buyer first. Then decide whether the piece belongs in your own paid publication or in an editor-reviewed program. This is a practical route for a creator who uses AI tools, wants to earn from writing rather than building an app, and needs a way to judge opportunities without pretending every program is open to everyone.

## Two different markets

Your own audience is one market. You decide the promise, the price, and the release date. An editor-reviewed program is another: it has a brief, an acceptance bar, and sometimes an exclusivity rule.

That distinction matters for a YouTube script writer. A reader whose upload schedule stalls at the scripting stage may pay for a tested sequence that turns a rough idea into a recordable script. They do not need another general essay on AI. They need to know what to ask, what to cut, and what must stay in human hands.

Apify’s Write for Apify page is unusually clear about the second market. Its program calls for work based on things writers have actually built or problems they have solved. A quarterly call sets the themes; writers submit through Discord; the company says it pays $500 after review and publication preparation. It also says previously published articles are not eligible. Publishing the same piece on a newsletter first can therefore eliminate that route.

TECHi is worth checking only with the eligibility line in view. Its free Author tier says applicants need one million combined followers across listed social platforms. That is not a verdict on the writing. It is a distribution requirement. If you are below it, do not build this week’s plan around it.

## A four-step article product

### Start with a failure you can prove

Avoid a topic such as “AI YouTube script writing tips.” It gives a reader no reason to believe the advice survived contact with work.

Start narrower: a script became too dense to read aloud, so its opening, argument, and on-screen direction were separated. That has a concrete before, a change, and a result the reader can test. If you did not do the work yourself, do not turn it into a pitch for an editor-reviewed program. Apify specifically asks for working code and real examples in its submission flow.

### Give away the decision, not the whole deliverable

The free section should show the problem, the change, and who should skip the method. For YouTube script writing jobs, that might mean showing how a vague brief becomes a viewer, an outcome, and a constraint before any prose is generated.

This is also where AI earns its place. It can expose missing assumptions and produce alternate structures. It cannot tell you whether the presenter can say the line naturally, whether the claim is defensible, or whether the footage exists. Those are editing decisions.

### Sell reusable materials

A paid article should reduce work, not merely contain more paragraphs. Useful materials include a brief-to-script question set, a template that separates the opening from the argument and visuals, examples of output rejected in editing, and a checklist for publication opportunities.

That is a more useful answer than asking for the best AI for YouTube script writing. The tool matters less than a repeatable decision sequence and a record of what you changed.

### Check for conflicts before release

Before publishing, answer four plain questions: Is the article required to be unpublished? Does it fit the current brief? Can you demonstrate the work? What exactly triggers payment?

If any answer is missing, pause the external submission. Publish a different piece to your own audience, or do the underlying work first. A rushed submission is not proof of a writing business.

## A one-video test for a YouTube script writer

Use one existing video idea. Write the viewer’s desired outcome in one sentence. Ask the AI for separate fields for the opening thirty seconds, the supporting argument, and the visuals. Read the result aloud, revise only the parts that fail in the mouth, and keep the change log.

That small log becomes evidence for the next article, the next client brief, or a future application. It also prevents ai YouTube script writing from becoming a polite way to ship unedited text.

If your scripting is delaying uploads, try the workflow built for that constraint: [Capafy’s YouTube script writer](https://capafy.ai/agent/7686597754?product_id=capafy-skills&run_id=20261017-223414&artifact_id=article-en&variant_id=choose-writing-market-first&click_id=20261017-223414-article-en&ct=article-youtube-script-writer)

## What to do next

Do not treat paid programs as a generic list of places to submit. Match one verified piece of work to one set of conditions. If the conditions do not fit yet, publish the useful method for your own reader, track what changes in their work, and use that evidence when the next market is actually open.
